 Once Upon A Farm sued over Tractor Wheels recall and toddler marketing
 By Elizabeth Crawford 19-Nov-2026 Last updated on 19-Nov-2026 at 14:25 GMT 
 Once Upon A Farm recalled all varieties and lots of its Tractor Wheels soft-baked bars following reports of choking incidents involving toddlers. (Image: Once Upon a Farm) Three consumers allege the children’s food maker misled parents by marketing its Tractor Wheels bars as suitable for toddlers and failed to adequately compensate customers following its nationwide recall
 Children’s food manufacturer Once Upon A Farm faces a proposed class action lawsuit alleging it misled consumers by marketing its Tractor Wheels soft-baked bars as safe and suitable for toddlers and mishandled the recall process, despite the company swiftly recalling the entire snack line following reports of choking incidents.
 Three customers who live in Oregon, Washington, DC, and New York joined forces to file a class action lawsuit in federal court Nov. 17 on behalf of themselves and “all others similarly situated,” who they say were misled by Once Upon A Farm marketing that claimed the Tractor Wheels were safe for toddlers who can “self-feed with fingers,” “have back teeth to chew” and can “bite through various textures.”
 Contrary to these on-pack marketing claims, the plaintiffs allege “the products are so dangerous and defectively designed and constructed that the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA) recalled the products” after it received several reports that toddlers suffered complete airway obstruction while consuming the product.
 The agency warned consumers Nov. 3 not to buy or serve the product because it said, “when chewed, the product reportedly forms a dry, sticky mass that standard choking interventions – including back blows and the Heimlich maneuver – may fail to dislodge.”
 The company quickly and transparently recalled all of the Tractor Wheels soft-baked bars, rather than only select lots, increased its consumer relations team to respond to inquires “promptly and personally” and offered a full refund for product returned where it was purchased.
 The lawsuit alleges the recall was “woefully inadequate,” in part because mixed messages from FDA, the company and retailers led to many consumers throwing away leftover products and therefore unable to obtain a refund. It also alleges because the company did not offer refunds for products that consumers ate or threw away it retained “tens of millions of revenue … due to its duped consumers.”
 Explore related questions
 The lawsuit adds the sale of the products were “incredibly lucrative” for the company, which told investors that they accounted for about 18% of its year-to-date sales, which the plaintiffs’ estimate is about $50 million annually. 
 From recall response to legal liability
 The consumer sentiment and financial impact of the recall in the lawsuit contradicts that reported by Once Upon A Farm executives.
 During the company’s third-quarter earnings call Nov. 12, CEO John Foraker said the company received “ positive retailer and consumer sentiments around the company’s decision to prioritize safety through the voluntary recall.”
 The company also estimated the recall would cost up to $30 million, which cut into its 2026 guidance. 
 The lawsuit filed this week also could expose Once Upon A Farm to financial liability beyond the cost of the recalled products. The plaintiffs are seeking statutory and actual damages under consumer protection laws in Oregon, New York and Washington, DC, as well as restitution, punitive damages where permitted and attorneys’ fees. The complaint does not specify a total monetary damages figure.
 In addition to seeking nationwide class certification for customers who bought the bars within the last four years and sub-classes for each location the plaintiffs represent, the lawsuit demands a jury trial, which could contribute significant costs and expose the company to additional reputational damage. 
 What the lawsuit could mean for food manufacturers
 While the outcome of the case is uncertain, it raises significant questions for the wider food industry. 
 For example, even though Once Upon A Farm’s recall was broad, the allegations raise questions about whether a product recall adequately addresses consumer losses, particularly when consumers follow regulatory advice to discard potentially hazardous products but subsequently find themselves unable to obtain a refund. 
 It also raises the question of what responsibility manufacturers have for age-appropriate product positioning, given the focus on the toddler-specific marketing used by the Tractor Wheels before they were identified as a potential fatal choking hazard. 
 Finally, the case underscores the risk companies face of substantial consumer litigation even when they proactively acknowledge a failure and take corrective action.
